sources.title: Florida Museum: Florida Native People teacher guide
sources.note: Indexed original PDF, Northern Florida’s Early Native People FAQ: Timucua linguistic grouping versus Apalachee, Saturiwa/Utina/Potano examples. No precise prehistoric date assigned to language.

sources.title: Florida Museum: The Timucua in St. Augustine
sources.note: Full indexed original archaeological interpretation, Seloy, matrilineal chiefdoms, pottery and shell tools. Does not treat de Bry pictures as direct ethnographic photographs or repeat blanket five-century cultural stasis.

sources.title: National Park Service: Timucua Daily Life
sources.note: Full indexed official interpretation, circular thatched homes, woven walls with clay, village squares and subsistence.

sources.title: National Park Service: Timucuan Ways of Life
sources.note: Full indexed official interpretation, Food and Religion. Plant-based healing and childbirth assistance attributed as historical practices, no efficacy claim or unsupported owl-clan inference.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Students unearth rare, centuries-year-old pot at local mission site
sources.note: Full indexed primary excavation-team account: Potano displacement 1585, mission 1606 to 1706, intact small pot, faint scorch marks and absence of cooking residue; meal bones. Exact recent excavation year not inferred from relative publication metadata.

sources.title: Gifford Waters and Charles Cobb: Baptizing Spring, Comparative Mission Archaeology Portal
sources.note: Direct research synthesis, August 2019, structures C and D and associated hearths/trash/storage pits. Canonical redirect from Florida Museum portal. Site generally attributed San Juan de Guacara; no definitive attribution needed in prose.

sources.title: National Park Service: Missions in Northeast Florida
sources.note: Full indexed official page, mission tribute, drafted labor and 1650s revolt. Does not adopt anomalous 1760s date for mission-destroying attacks; independent 1702 chronology used.

sources.title: Comparative Mission Archaeology Portal: Mission Nombre de Dios
sources.note: Direct archaeological documentary synthesis, Overview and Documentary Evidence: Doña Ana and daughter, destruction, refugees and 1763 migration to Cuba.

sources.title: John Hessler, Library of Congress: Chi Mobi, Writing Timucua in Seventeenth Century Florida
sources.note: Full indexed institutional collection research, reproduced sentence and translation from Pareja’s 1613 Confessionario. Direct open failed, exact indexed original query returns full article. Quote total 23 words including Timucua and English; missionary pejorative religious framing explicitly attributed.

sources.title: National Park Service: A Walk Through the History of Fort George Island
sources.note: Full indexed official timeline, San Juan del Puerto destroyed by James Moore in 1702; no unrelated erroneous timeline claims used.

sources.title: National Park Service, Fort Matanzas: Women
sources.note: Direct page and indexed section María Magdalena Chrisístomo-Balthazar, eighteenth-century Mocama Timucua mother and African father, free daughters and marriages. Avoids assumption every Timucua family had same experience.

sources.title: National Park Service: Indigenous Cultural Landscapes Study, Lower Susquehanna Area
sources.note: Direct primary regional research PDF. Printed pages 25 to 26 locate circa 1500 North Branch communities, pages 24 to 25 discuss family inference, printed page 30 discusses survivors and 1845 claim by people living among Oneida. Does not repeat erroneous Christmas Eve massacre date, absolute disappearance or giant stature.

sources.title: Library of Congress Subject Headings: Susquehanna Indians
sources.note: Full indexed official authority cross-reference: Susquehannock Indians USE Susquehanna Indians, likewise language. Used as identity evidence only, not proof every Susquehanna Valley people was Susquehannock.

sources.title: Susquehanna National Heritage Area: Susquehannock Native Landscape
sources.note: Direct full institutional account, trade paths, longhouses, Schultz food remains and face pots. Does not use absolute annihilation or certain Shenks Ferry absorption/motivation claims.

sources.title: H. Trawick Ward: Archaeological Background, Excavating Occaneechi Town
sources.note: Direct scholarly comparative analysis, paragraphs on Ibaugh, Strickler and Conestoga. Cultural attribution and dates kept specific; imported possessions do not prove wealth or every household’s practice.

sources.title: Celeste Marie Gagnon and Sara K. Becker: Native Lives in Colonial Times
sources.note: Direct abstract plus full indexed primary article, Historical Archaeology 54 (2020), pages 262 to 285. 102 individuals, two samples, cautious association of reduced stress with 1652 treaty. Does not treat sample as census or absence of skeletal violence as proof of peaceful times.

sources.title: National Park Service: Winter, an Important Time of Year for the Susquehannock People
sources.note: Direct Paul Nevin lecture report, explicitly comparative reconstruction using archaeology and other Iroquoian lifeways. Prose preserves inference, not direct attestation of a particular winter ceremony. Article’s denial of descendant community excluded, contradicted by newer Heritage Area descendant project and historical documentation.

sources.title: Marianne Mithun: Stalking the Susquehannocks
sources.note: Direct author-uploaded full 1981 International Journal of American Linguistics article. Section 6 appendix, Vocabulary of the Minque language (Holm 1702): Generoo. Good friend. Introduction describes Campanius 1642 to 1648 and 1696/1702 publications. Exact selected entry readable despite OCR corruption elsewhere; no reconstructed phrase.

sources.title: Pennsylvania DCNR: History of Susquehannock State Park
sources.note: Direct state history, 1675 fort siege and negotiators, return to valley and 1763 Conestoga killings. Does not adopt claim last two people dying ended all Susquehannock descent.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Single broad linguistic-cultural map label, not a unified state or association with separate local peoples. First world_1492 polygon bbox [-83.8466,28.2600,-80.5526,31.9678]. Preserve imported 1492 to 1650, foreground distinct chiefdoms and later mission chronology. Potano/Seloy evidence explicitly local; neither claimed as universal Timucua behavior. No universal extinction assertion or unsourced present-day recognized tribal-government claim.

Same-people label association supported by Library of Congress authority cross-references and compatible decoded geographic phases. First susquehannock world_1492 bbox [-79.0082,38.3051,-75.7322,42.6502]; susquehanna world_1530 bbox [-78.7886,39.3615,-75.3650,42.4040]. Earlier outline is too broad and southward for a precise circa-1500 homeland; opening explicitly warns, lower-valley evidence dated later. Do not absorb Shenks Ferry or other Susquehanna Valley peoples. Preserve first imported interval1492 to1500 and second1530 to1650; neither marks extinction. Original map spelling remains index identity; shared override uses historical people name.
